test_cases.question: What makes two or more organizations joint controllers under GDPR?
test_cases.answer: Two or more organizations become joint controllers when they jointly determine the purposes and means of processing personal data. In such cases, they must transparently determine their respective responsibilities for compliance with the Regulation, particularly regarding data subject rights and their duties to provide information under Articles 13 and 14. The arrangement may also designate a contact point for data subjects.
test_cases.supporting_quote: Where two or more controllers jointly determine the purposes and means of processing, they shall be joint controllers. They shall in a transparent manner determine their respective responsibilities for compliance with the obligations under this Regulation, in particular as regards the exercising of the rights of the data subject and their respective duties to provide the information referred to in Articles 13 and 14

test_cases.question: Must joint controllers inform data subjects about their internal arrangement?
test_cases.answer: Yes. The arrangement between joint controllers must duly reflect their respective roles and relationships vis-à-vis the data subjects, and the essence of that arrangement must be made available to the data subject.
test_cases.supporting_quote: The arrangement referred to in paragraph 1 shall duly reflect the respective roles and relationships of the joint controllers vis-à-vis the data subjects. The essence of the arrangement shall be made available to the data subject.
key_phrases: made available to the data subject

test_cases.question: If two companies have an internal agreement about who handles data subject requests, does that limit which controller a data subject can contact?
test_cases.answer: No. Regardless of any arrangement between the joint controllers, the data subject may exercise their GDPR rights in respect of and against each of the controllers. The internal agreement does not restrict the data subject's ability to invoke their rights against any joint controller.
test_cases.supporting_quote: Irrespective of the terms of the arrangement referred to in paragraph 1, the data subject may exercise his or her rights under this Regulation in respect of and against each of the controllers

test_cases.question: When are joint controllers allowed to skip creating their own arrangement and rely on existing law instead?
test_cases.answer: Controllers may rely on Union or Member State law to determine their respective responsibilities instead of creating their own arrangement, but only when such law already applies to the controllers and specifies how their responsibilities should be allocated. Otherwise, they must establish their own transparent arrangement.
test_cases.supporting_quote: unless, and in so far as, the respective responsibilities of the controllers are determined by Union or Member State law to which the controllers are subject

b2b_relevance: CRITICAL - Article 26 governs partnerships, integrations, and shared platforms. Essential for: partnership agreements, platform operator relationships, API/data sharing arrangements, and determining who responds to data subject requests. Key takeaways: (1) 'Jointly determine purposes and means' is the test, (2) Essence of arrangement must be public, (3) Data subjects can go after ANY joint controller, (4) Internal allocation doesn't protect you externally.
